steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on open-ended visual quality comparison with large multi-modality models. It should motivate comparison over absolute quality ratings, explain how we build an instruction-tuning dataset without human labels, introduce the model and the multi-image benchmark, and end with a contributions list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. IQA and its recent move to open-ended evaluation with LMMs
2. Why comparison: ambiguity of absolute evaluations
3. Gaps in existing data and models; collecting data from weak supervisors (Co-Instruct)
4. Image-text interleaved format and model structure; results of Co-Instruct
5. MICBench: evaluating comparison beyond two images
6. Contributions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text: Image quality assessment (IQA) is an important area in visual computing. It gives effective recommendation on high-quality visual contents, and it also gives valuable guidance for potential improvements. Recently some pioneer studies explored using large multi-modality models (LMMs, e.g. GPT-4V) to expand IQA from just giving a scalar score (e.g. 3.457) to open-ended scenarios, where the model can respond to open-range questions and give detailed reasonings and not only an overall score. These studies emulate the human ability on IQA quite well, but they also have the same drawback as humans, which is the ambiguity of absolute evaluations. For example, in Fig. 2 (a), different human observers have different standards on the exposure level of single images, so they give diversified absolute evaluations. But when they are asked to compare the exposure level of the images, all observers agree with the rank (1)>(2)>(3)>(4) (Fig. 2 (b)). All the observers also agree that (1) has the highest exposure, even though not all of them choose the option high when they evaluate it on its own. Because of this, comparison has been a traditional human study setting for quality evaluation and it is used by a wide range of existing subjective studies. Also, to avoid the ambiguity, comparative settings are mostly used when IQA algorithms are applied for improvement guidance. Comparison is widely recognized as significant for IQA, but existing related datasets and methods are generally based on overall quality comparison and they do not extend to open-ended scenarios. At the same time, open-source LMMs are usually only fine-tuned with single image instruction tuning datasets, and they were shown to lack enough capability even on two image comparison settings. So there is a clear need for a specific instruction tuning dataset for visual quality comparison, but it is too expensive to collect such a dataset from humans. To avoid the costly human labor, we propose a different strategy to collect the training dataset, which we call Collaborative Instruction Tuning from Weak Supervisors (Co-Instruct). We use two non-perfect supervisors. The first one is Merge2Compare (Fig. 3 (a)). It starts from single image quality descriptions on 19K images that were labeled by humans in the Q-Pathway dataset. We randomly match them into 100K groups (2-4 images per group) and remove the most similar descriptions with a text embedding model. Then we prompt a single-modal large language model (LLM) to compare the multiple human descriptions in a group, and "merge" them into 100K pseudo comparisons. The second one is Teach2Compare (Fig. 3 (b)). We see that GPT-4V has especially high accuracy on pairwise settings among the existing LMMs, so following existing practices we use GPT-4V responses to expand our dataset further. We collect 9K unlabeled images and randomly match them into 30K image groups (also 2-4 images per group), and we get GPT-4V responses on both caption-like general comparisons and question-answer pairs for comparisons. By putting together Q-Instruct-200K (on single images), Merge2Compare, and Teach2Compare, we construct the Co-Instruct-562K, which is the first instruction tuning dataset for open-ended visual quality comparison. 4. Input format and model - image-text interleaved format to refer to each image: User: The first image: The second image: ... Assistant: - LLaVA structure (linear projection of visual embeddings) would exceed LLM context window with multiple images - visual abstractor: 1,025 -> 65 tokens per image, then concatenated with text embeddings - Co-Instruct: up to 86% better than baseline, 61% better than SOTA open-source LMM - surpasses GPT-4V teacher on MCQ benchmarks, matches GPT-4V on detailed reasoning 5. MICBench - Q-Bench series covers single images and pairs; nothing beyond two images - MICBench: 2,000 MCQs, groups of three or four images (each half) - over half are Which questions (e.g. which image has highest clarity?) - most important for comparison - also Yes-or-No and What/How/How-Many etc. -> holistic setting 6. Contributions - Co-Instruct-562K dataset from two weak supervisors; public; expands open-source LMM comparison ability - Co-Instruct model: interleaved input, outperforms existing methods and even GPT-4V; open weights - MICBench: first benchmark for comparison on more than two images; 2,000 MCQs

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text: Image quality assessment (IQA) is an important area in visual computing. It gives effective recommendation on high-quality visual contents, and it also gives valuable guidance for potential improvements. Recently some pioneer studies explored using large multi-modality models (LMMs, e.g. GPT-4V) to expand IQA from just giving a scalar score (e.g. 3.457) to open-ended scenarios, where the model can respond to open-range questions and give detailed reasonings and not only an overall score. These studies emulate the human ability on IQA quite well, but they also have the same drawback as humans, which is the ambiguity of absolute evaluations. For example, in Fig. 2 (a), different human observers have different standards on the exposure level of single images, so they give diversified absolute evaluations. But when they are asked to compare the exposure level of the images, all observers agree with the rank (1)>(2)>(3)>(4) (Fig. 2 (b)). All the observers also agree that (1) has the highest exposure, even though not all of them choose the option high when they evaluate it on its own. Because of this, comparison has been a traditional human study setting for quality evaluation and it is used by a wide range of existing subjective studies. Also, to avoid the ambiguity, comparative settings are mostly used when IQA algorithms are applied for improvement guidance. Comparison is widely recognized as significant for IQA, but existing related datasets and methods are generally based on overall quality comparison and they do not extend to open-ended scenarios. At the same time, open-source LMMs are usually only fine-tuned with single image instruction tuning datasets, and they were shown to lack enough capability even on two image comparison settings. So there is a clear need for a specific instruction tuning dataset for visual quality comparison, but it is too expensive to collect such a dataset from humans. To avoid the costly human labor, we propose a different strategy to collect the training dataset, which we call Collaborative Instruction Tuning from Weak Supervisors (Co-Instruct). We use two non-perfect supervisors. The first one is Merge2Compare (Fig. 3 (a)). It starts from single image quality descriptions on 19K images that were labeled by humans in the Q-Pathway dataset. We randomly match them into 100K groups (2-4 images per group) and remove the most similar descriptions with a text embedding model. Then we prompt a single-modal large language model (LLM) to compare the multiple human descriptions in a group, and "merge" them into 100K pseudo comparisons. The second one is Teach2Compare (Fig. 3 (b)). We see that GPT-4V has especially high accuracy on pairwise settings among the existing LMMs, so following existing practices we use GPT-4V responses to expand our dataset further. We collect 9K unlabeled images and randomly match them into 30K image groups (also 2-4 images per group), and we get GPT-4V responses on both caption-like general comparisons and question-answer pairs for comparisons. By putting together Q-Instruct-200K (on single images), Merge2Compare, and Teach2Compare, we construct the Co-Instruct-562K, which is the first instruction tuning dataset for open-ended visual quality comparison. To refer correctly to each specific image during the conversation, we define a specific image-text interleaved format that handles multi-image cases, as follows: User: The first image: The second image: ... Assistant: Also, since we need to feed multiple images together to the LLM decoder, using the most popular LLaVA structure, which linearly projects the visual embeddings, will exceed the context window of the language models and cause errors. So we use an alternative visual abstractor structure that first reduces the visual token length (from 1,025 to 65 tokens per image), and then concatenates them with the text embeddings to pass to the language decoders. By learning from the Co-Instruct-562K dataset with this specially-designed input structure, we get the Co-Instruct model. It has up to 86% improvements over its baseline, and it is 61% better than the state-of-the-art open-source LMM. More importantly, even though GPT-4V is one of its teachers, it still surpasses the GPT-4V teacher in a variety of multi-choice question (MCQ) benchmarks, and it matches GPT-4V ability in scenarios that need detailed language reasonings. After training Co-Instruct, another concern we have is that there are not many evaluation settings on multi-image comparison. The Q-Bench series covers multiple formats on single images and image pairs, but there is no existing evaluation scenario for quality comparison beyond two images. To complement this, we construct the MICBench. The MICBench contains 2,000 multi-choice questions (MCQ) that compare the quality or related attributes among a group of three or four images (each half). Over half of the questions are Which questions (e.g. which image has highest clarity?). Which questions aim to extract an image with a specific quality-related appearance from a group, so they are the most important questions related to image comparison. Besides Which questions, the MICBench also includes Yes-or-No questions and other question types (What/How/How-Many, etc), so it gives a holistic benchmark setting for multi-image quality comparison. In summary, we do a systematical study towards open-ended visual quality comparison. Our contributions are three-fold: - 1. We construct the Co-Instruct-562K, the first instruction-tuning dataset for visual quality comparison. Its data is collected from two "weak supervisors", Merge2Compare (LLM-merged comparisons) and Teach2Compare (GPT-4V pseudo-labeled comparisons), and our public dataset significantly expands the capabilities of open-source LMMs on visual comparative settings. - 2. We propose the Co-Instruct, the most capable model for open-ended visual comparison. It uses the image-text interleaved input format and is fine-tuned with the Co-Instruct-562K dataset, and it significantly outperforms existing methods (and even GPT-4V) in multiple open-ended visual comparison tasks. Because it has open weights, it can be applied more broadly than proprietary models. - 3. We construct the MICBench, the first benchmark to evaluate LMMs for quality comparison on multiple images (more than two). It covers 2,000 diverse-type open-range MCQs about visual quality comparison among three or four images. The MICBench contributes to more holistic evaluation studies on the visual quality comparison problem.

steps.text: Image quality assessment (IQA) has been an important domain in visual computing, as it provides effective recommendation [1] on high-quality visual contents and valuable guidance [2,3,4] for potential improvements. Most recently, several pioneer studies [5,6,7] have explored large multi-modality models (LMMs, e.g. GPT-4V) [8,9,10,11,12,13], on expanding IQA from giving a scalar score (e.g. 3.457) to the open-ended scenarios, that allows evaluations in response to open-range questions, and provide detailed reasonings beyond an overall score. While these studies emulate human ability on IQA well, they also suffer from the same drawback as human: ambiguity on absolute evaluations. For instance, as shown in Fig. 2 (a), different human observers hold different standards on the exposure level on single images, and henceforth provide diversified absolute evaluations. Nevertheless, while asked to compare the exposure level of the images, all observers agree with the rank (1)>(2)>(3)>(4) (Fig. 2 (b)); all observers also agree that (1) has the highest exposure, though not all choose the option high while evaluating it independently. Because of this, comparison has been a traditional human study setting for quality evaluation [14] and adopted by a wide range of existing subjective studies [15,16,17,2,18]. Furthermore, to avoid the ambiguity, the comparative settings are also mostly adopted [4,2] while applying IQA algorithms for improvement guidance. While comparison has widely-recognized significance for IQA, existing related datasets [15] and methods [19,20] are generally based on overall quality comparison and have not extended to the open-ended scenarios; on the other hand, open-source LMMs [5,10,12] are usually only fine-tuned with single image instruction tuning datasets [21,22,23] and proved to lack enough capability even on two image comparison settings [24,25]. While these gaps have clearly indicated the need of a specific instruction tuning dataset for visual quality comparison, collecting such a dataset from human is too expensive. To avoid costly human labors, we propose an alternative strategy to collect the training dataset, named Collaborative Instruction Tuning from Weak Supervisors (Co-Instruct). Specifically, we adopt two non-perfect supervisors: 1) Merge2Compare (Fig. 3 (a)). Originated from single image quality descriptions on 19K images as labeled by human in the Q-Pathway [5] dataset, we randomly match them into 100K groups (2-4 images per group) with removing the most similar descriptions with an text embedding model [26]. Then, we prompt a single-modal large language model (LLM) [27] to compare multiple human descriptions in a group, and “merge” them into 100K pseudo comparisons. 2) Teach2Compare (Fig. 3 (b)). Observing that GPT-4V has especially high accuracy on pairwise settings [25,24] among existing LMMs, following existing practices [28,29], we leverage GPT-4V responses to further expand our dataset. We collect 9K unlabeled images and randomly match into 30K image groups (also 2-4 images per group), and obtain GPT-4V responses on both caption-like general comparisons and question-answer pairs for comparisons. By integrating Q-Instruct-200K [5] (on single images), Merge2Compare, and Teach2Compare, we construct the Co-Instruct-562K, the first instruction tuning dataset for open-ended visual quality comparison. To correctly refer to each specific image during conversation, we define a specific image-text interleaved format [13] to handle multi-image cases, as follows: User: The first image: The second image: ... Assistant: Moreover, as we need to feed multiple images together to the LLM decoder, adopting the most popular LLaVA [21,30,10] structure that linearly projects visual embeddings will exceed the context window of the language models [31] and cause errors. So we adopt an alternative visual abstractor structure [11] to first reduce visual token length (from 1,025 to 65 tokens per image), and then concatenate them with text embeddings to pass to language decoders. By learning from the Co-Instruct-562K dataset and the specially-designed input structure, we present the Co-Instruct, with up to 86% improvements than its baseline [11], and 61% better than the state-of-the-art open-source LMM. More importantly, despite using GPT-4V as one of its teachers, it still surpasses the GPT-4V teacher in a variety of multi-choice question (MCQ) benchmarks, and matches GPT-4V ability in scenarios requiring detailed language reasonings. After training the model Co-Instruct, another concern is the lack of abundant evaluation settings on multi-image comparison: while Q-Bench [6,24] series have covered multiple formats on single images and image pairs, there is no existing evaluation scenario for quality comparison beyond two images. To complement this evaluation setting, we construct the MICBench. Specifically, the MICBench contains 2,000 multi-choice questions (MCQ) comparing the quality or related attributes among a group of three or four images (each half), in which over half of the questions are Which questions (e.g. which image has highest clarity?). Which questions are the most important questions related to image comparison, as they aim to extract an image with a specific quality-related appearance from a group. Despite Which questions, the MICBench also includes Yes-or-No questions and other question types (What/How/How-Many, etc) to provide a holistic benchmark setting for multi-image quality comparison. In summary, we conduct a systematical study towards open-ended visual quality comparison. Our contributions are three-fold: - 1. We construct the first instruction-tuning dataset for visual quality comparison, the Co-Instruct-562K. With data collected from two “weak supervisors”, Merge2Compare (LLM-merged comparisons) and Teach2Compare (GPT-4V pseudo-labeled comparisons), our public dataset significantly expands the capabilities of open-source LMMs on visual comparative settings. - 2. We propose the most capable model for open-ended visual comparison, the Co-Instruct. With image-text interleaved input format and fine-tuned with the Co-Instruct-562K dataset, it significantly outperforms existing methods (and even GPT-4V) in multiple open-ended visual comparison tasks. Since it has open weights, it can be applied more broadly than proprietary models. - 3. We construct the benchmark, the MICBench, as the first benchmark to evaluate LMMs for quality comparison on multiple images (more than two). It covers 2,000 diverse-type open-range MCQs related to visual quality comparison among three or four images. The MICBench contributes to more holistic evaluation studies on the visual quality comparison problem.
